cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-43-christ.summary: In the centre of the heavens the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos lies asleep on a curtained bed attended by angels, a literal picture of the cry 'Awake, why sleepest thou, O Lord? arise'. Below, the armed psalmist and his soldiers stand in a walled enclosure, their useless weapons heaped before them, while people lie prostrate before an altar and the slain are dragged away. The image of the sleeping Lord recalls Christ asleep in the storm-tossed boat.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-43-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server. This folio carries two drawings; the crop shows the one for this text.

cur:monumental-oberzell-widow-of-nain.summary: Before the gate of the city of Nain, Christ, followed by the apostles, stretches out his hand towards the bier on which the young man sits up, while the bearers stop and the mourning widow kneels at Christ's feet. Painted against a soft blue sky, it is the first of the raisings from the dead that close the cycle.
facts: The eight miracle scenes on the nave walls of St George, Oberzell, were rediscovered under later plaster in 1880; they are dated either to about 900 (late Carolingian) or, in the prevailing view, to the late 10th century (Ottonian).

Apart from Müstair, St George is the only church north of the Alps in the former Empire to preserve so complete a cycle of early medieval wall painting; the sequence runs from the entrance along the north wall to the altar and back along the south wall, culminating in the Raising of Lazarus.
In each scene Christ, larger than the other figures, stands at the left with a gesture of blessing directed into the narrative, except in two scenes where he appears twice.

Q29385468.summary: An openwork cage of gilded grapevines encloses a plain silver cup, and among the vines sit twelve figures: two images of Christ, the others variously identified as apostles or as ancient sages who foretold his coming. Birds, a lamb, snails and other small creatures fill the branches, evoking Christ's words 'I am the vine; you are the branches'. Once sensationally claimed to be the Holy Grail itself, it is now valued as a superb work of early Byzantine silverwork.
facts: It was reportedly found near Antioch around 1910, and when it was first published in 1916 the plain inner cup was proclaimed to be the cup of the Last Supper.
It was exhibited as the Holy Grail at the 1933 Chicago World's Fair, and was acquired for The Cloisters in 1950.
Its shape has more recently been identified with that of standing lamps used in sixth-century churches, which is why the Metropolitan Museum places 'Chalice' in quotation marks.
The vine-scroll imagery recalls both the Eucharist and the Gospel of John's image of Christ as the true vine.
Q29385468.notes: Christ's presence rests on the Met's statement that two of the twelve figures 'are thought to be' Christ; they cannot be distinguished in the thumbnail. The other ten have been read as apostles or classical philosophers. Authenticity has at times been questioned.

princeton:17163.summary: This narrow tapestry-woven band in red, yellow, blue and cream shows a column of figures framed by a scrolling vine border: a pair of heads at the top, a frontal nimbed figure holding something dark against the chest, and below it two figures pressed together in an embrace. Princeton's subject terms identify Christ, Mary and saints among them. Such bands once decorated tunics and furnishings in Coptic Egypt.
facts: Princeton dates the fragment to the 8th–9th century and records it as wool and linen, measuring 36 by 5.4 cm.
It was published in the 1986 exhibition catalogue 'Byzantium at Princeton', and the Index of Christian Art holds a set of photographs of it.

links.label: Princeton University Art Museum object page

princeton:17163.notes: Christ's presence rests on the museum's subject terms; the stylised figures cannot be identified with certainty from the photograph. The embracing pair might be a Visitation, but this is not confirmed, so no scripture is given.

Q734834.summary: In the lower central panel, Christ appears as the Lamb of God standing upon an altar, his blood flowing into a chalice, adored by angels, prophets, apostles, martyrs and virgins converging across a paradise meadow. Above, an enthroned figure in crimson — read variously as Christ the King or God the Father — presides between the Virgin and John the Baptist. With its astonishing detail and luminous oil glazes, the polyptych is often called the first great masterpiece of Northern Renaissance painting.
facts: The 'Just Judges' panel was stolen in 1934 and has never been recovered; the panel in place today is a copy by Jef Van der Veken.
A restoration of the lower panels completed in January 2020 removed later overpaint and revealed the Lamb's original, strikingly human-like face.

Art historian Noah Charney counts 13 crimes and seven thefts in its history: it was carried off to Paris after the French Revolution, seized on Hitler's orders in 1942, and recovered from the Altaussee salt mine in 1945.
Scholars have counted some 75 to 81 different plants painted in the meadow around the Lamb, many identifiable with botanical accuracy.

commons:115196098.summary: The child Jesus stands on a rock between Mary and Joseph, holding their hands, while above him the Holy Spirit descends as a dove and God the Father looks down among clouds and angels. The vertical line of the heavenly Trinity crosses the horizontal line of the earthly 'trinity' of the Holy Family precisely at the figure of Christ. Murillo's gentle, glowing style made the scene a beloved meditation on the Incarnation, uniting heaven and earth in a child.
facts: The composition forms a cross, with the boy Jesus at the intersection — often read as a quiet foreshadowing of the Passion.
The 'Two Trinities' was rarely painted in 17th-century Spain; the scene is not a specific Gospel episode, though it echoes the finding of the twelve-year-old Jesus in the Temple (Luke 2:41–50).
Christ stands on a sharp-edged rock, possibly symbolizing an altar or Christ as the 'cornerstone', while Joseph holds his flowering rod, the sign of his betrothal to Mary.
Known as 'The Pedroso Murillo' after the family that owned it in Cádiz by 1708, the painting reached England in 1810 and was bought by the National Gallery in 1837.
